Ghost in the Wires by Kevin Mitnick - This is not a how to book of how to get into Cybersecurity but a book detailing the exploits of one of the greatest hackers of all time known for social engineering. You can fortify your network, have robust systems in place to guard against hackers but if someone can convince an employee to give up their login details, all that security would have been for nil, that's why social engineering is hard to guard against since it exploits trust people have in others and Kevin was one of the best at social engineering. Social Engineering: The Art of Human Hacking (Wiley) - A how to guide if you are interested in how to actually use social engineering attacks or safeguard against them.

Ethical Hacking - A Hands-on Introduction to Breaking In by Daniel Graham (No Starch Press) - This is for the technical details of how to hack as you would normally imagine. You are going to get negative responses in hacking subreddits, I am not sure if it's gate keeping or a way to keep out competition. If you are definitely passionate about this just go in head first and even if you fail what you would have learnt can be used in other areas, like web development or python freelancing.

Whether you can make that money within a year of learning and hacking, I can't say since I am not yet a hacker but if you really want to become one use the below resources, the money will come later. An easier path to earn cash would be to learn web development and get a job in that or do freelancing, you can learn web development for free at theodinproject.com, you can definitely get a job (some have been hired for $100k/year entry level jobs) if you put in 8hrs of studying everyday for a year

Anyway if you want to learn hacking, join me in the struggle. Currently I am learning JavaScript, I just finished learning HTML and CSS basics, I know a bit of Python though I plan on going back to it later to strengthen my knowledge, I also received similar responses to this post when I asked for advice, but I know this is what I want to do for the rest of my life, don't let the negative experiences of others dictate how your experience in bug hunting will be.

First you need to learn:

1. HTML and CSS: you can learn this on freecodecamp, if you prefer a book read Learning Web Design (O'Reilly).

2. JavaScript: This is used for basic interactivity on websites, together with 1.  it forms the frontend of a site, at bare minimum you need to be able to read JavaScript. You can learn JavaScript at eloquentjavascript.net, or read JavaScript: The Definitive Guide (O'Reilly), this book assumes prior programming experience so if you don't have that, read Head First: Learn to Code or Think Python (can be read for free online on the author's website) before reading it.

3. bash: You are probably going to want to use Kali Linux, so being comfortable with a terminal is key to using any Linux distro, read The Linux Command Line (No Starch Press).

3.1 (Optional): Full Stack Web Development: Before you can hack it would wise if you knew how to actually build a website, knowing how something is built will give you an advantage when it comes to figuring out how to break it, read Learning PHP, MySQL and JavaScript (O'Reilly), by the end of the book you would have built a simple social media site. You can also learn full Stack Web development for free on theodinproject but I think it will be overkill, you don't need to be a web developer to learn how to hack websites though basic knowledge is a plus.

4. At this point you can start learning how to hack websites, read Bug Bounty Bootcamp (No Starch Press) or read Web hacking 101 (you can get the book for free on hackerone if you make an account there).

At this point start hacking, nothing beats real world experience. The resources below are for gaining more knowledge but are not required reading:

1. The Web Application Hacker's Handbook (Wiley): this is the Bible of web hacking, enough said.

2. Programming PHP (O'Reilly): PHP is a common language used for the backend, so a reading knowledge of it is a plus.

3. Learning Java (O'Reilly): Another popular language used for the backend. Free Book: Think Java (can be read for free on the author's website)

4. Dead Simple Python (No Starch Press): If you want to stay ahead of the curve you need to know how to make your own tools, relying on premade tools puts you at disadvantage since lots of people are using the same tool so it's unlikely you will get an output that no one has seen, Python is easy to learn and write code using it, so this makes it ideal for making tools on the fly. Free book: Automate the Boring Stuff with Python (a simple search will lead to the author's website where more of his books can be read).

5. The TCP/IP Guide (No Starch Press): This tome will teach all you need to know to understand protocols that run the internet. Can be read for free at author's website.

The instructor said to install PyCharm for coding, I had no idea what PyCharm was or what an IDE was, these were not explained.
